metaDescription: The best budget nugget ice makers for 2026, with honest notes on output claims, noise, cleaning and the upkeep that a cheap pebble ice machine demands.
expertTake: The Silonn 36 lb is our top budget pick because it has the fastest first-ice claim, a carry handle and a simple one-button routine. The Antarctic Star is the value pick for the lowest spend and a plain basket and scoop. Skip a nugget ice maker if you do not want a noisy countertop appliance that needs descaling every month or two.
introParagraphs: Nugget ice is the soft, chewable pebble ice that restaurants and convenience stores serve. Budget machines make it by freezing a thin layer of water on a cold cylinder and shaving it off with an auger, then dropping it into a basket.

The cheap versions all do the same trick, so the difference is in output honesty, noise, cleaning features and how often you must refill the reservoir. Plan for a weekly wipe and a monthly descale, because mineral scale is what ends these machines early.

products.name: Silonn Nugget Ice Maker Countertop 36 lb Day with Handle
products.description:
The Silonn is a sensible first nugget machine. It lists up to 36 lb of ice in a day, a first batch in about five minutes and a carry handle that lets you move it between a kitchen and a living room. Controls are limited to the basics, which is what most owners want.

Against the Antarctic Star it is quicker to the first scoop and a touch more output, but costs a little more. Against the EUHOMY 34 lb with a removable top cover it has a simpler build and less cleaning access. It ranks first because the output, speed and portability add up to the most useful budget package.

The daily figure is a peak rate measured over many hours, not what you get from a single fill. Expect to top up the reservoir several times a day if you use a lot of ice. Use filtered water to reduce scale, run a descaler cycle monthly and wipe the basket weekly. These machines are noisy during ice-making because the compressor and auger run together.

products.name: Antarctic Star Nugget Ice Maker Countertop with Scoop
products.description:
The Antarctic Star is the cheapest machine in this lineup, and it keeps things simple: a basket, a scoop and a first batch in about ten minutes. It is lightweight and has a handle, so it can sit on a counter or be tucked away between uses.

Against the Silonn it is slower to start and less proven, but it is the lowest cost way into nugget ice. Against the EUHOMY 35 lb stainless model it lacks a stainless body and a stated high output. It ranks second because the price advantage is real, though the extra five minutes before the first batch matters if you want ice quickly.

Treat it as a light-use machine for a couple of people. Fill the tank with filtered water, empty any leftover water before storing and wipe down the basket. The melted ice drains back into the reservoir, so keep an eye on the water level and discard stale water. If you want a machine that runs all day, step up to a higher output model.

products.description:
The Kismile pairs a stainless steel body with a 1.1 L tank and a claimed output of up to 35 lb per day. Its self-clean routine starts with a press of the power button, which makes the chore less annoying than a full strip-down.

Compared with the Silonn it has a smaller tank and slightly lower output, but it looks more at home on a counter. Against the EUHOMY 35 lb stainless model it is similar in claims, and the difference is mostly brand and support. It ranks third because the water tank is small and the maker is less established.

The 1.1 L tank means you will refill often if the machine runs for hours. Use filtered or distilled water to slow scale, and run the self-clean cycle each month. Wipe the stainless with a soft cloth to avoid fingerprints. Keep it level and a few inches from walls, since the compressor needs ventilation. Expect compressor noise while it makes ice.

The EUHOMY with a removable top cover is built around easier cleaning. The cover lifts off so you can reach the interior, and an auto-clean function handles part of the routine. A 1.2 qt tank and a first batch in about six minutes round out the package.

Against the Silonn it gives easier cleaning access but slightly lower output. Against the other EUHOMY at 35 lb it is a little faster to first ice. It ranks fourth because the clean-access benefit matters over years, though the immediate performance claims are similar to the leaders.

The key habit is regular descaling. Run the auto-clean cycle monthly, rinse the interior and leave the lid cracked when not in use to avoid musty smells. Use filtered water and empty the reservoir if you will not use it for several days. As with all budget units, the compressor is audible, so avoid placing it beside a bed or a TV.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Makers list pounds per 24 hours, such as 34 to 36 lb here, but that is a peak figure from running the machine for many hours. In real use, the basket holds a few pounds at a time. The common mistake is expecting a party's worth of ice from one cycle. In this lineup the Silonn lists 36 lb while the EUHOMY models list 34 and 35 lb.

The first batch takes about 5 to 10 minutes, with the Silonn at 5 and the Antarctic Star at 10. After that, ice arrives steadily. A shorter first batch matters if you use ice on demand. It matters little if the machine runs overnight. Water that starts cold, or filtered water kept in the fridge, shortens the wait a little, and a warm kitchen lengthens it.

A compressor, a pump and an auger work together, so these machines are louder than a fridge. Some premium models claim around 40 dB, while budget units are noisier. Place it away from sleeping areas. A rubber mat under the feet reduces vibration. Running it overnight in a kitchen next to a bedroom is the usual regret, so test the sound in your own space during the return window and plan to move it if it bothers you.

Scale is the main killer of ice makers. A removable cover, as on the EUHOMY 34 lb, and self-clean modes like the Kismile's help. Use filtered water and descale monthly. Skipping the descale cycle is the most common mistake. In a hard water area, the ice itself can taste chalky and the nuggets turn smaller and harder. A bottle of food-safe descaler lasts several cycles, so budget for it alongside the machine.

Tanks of 1.1 to 1.2 L run out quickly if you use a lot of ice. Melted ice drains back into the reservoir, so the machine recycles water, but the water gets stale after a day or two. Empty and refill with fresh water daily. Larger tanks mean fewer interruptions. When the water level drops, most of these machines stop and show a light, so you will not damage the pump, but you will have to stop what you are doing and fill it. Keep a jug of filtered water close by.

These are compact but need several inches of clearance for the compressor to vent. Place the machine on a level counter, away from heat sources. A built-in handle helps if you want to move it. Do not enclose it in a cabinet. Heat trapped behind the unit makes the compressor work harder and shortens the time between batches. Leave at least a hand's width at the back and sides, and keep it out of direct sun.

howWeEvaluated.title: Output and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the daily output and first-batch times on each spec sheet. The Silonn lists 36 lb and about 5 minutes while the Antarctic Star lists about 10 minutes. We rewarded honest claims over inflated numbers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning and scale
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at self-clean modes, cover design and reservoir access. Owner feedback patterns show scale buildup is the biggest long-term problem. The EUHOMY with a removable cover scored well here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and placement
howWeEvaluated.description: We read for decibel claims and body design. Compressor models are louder than ice cube trays. We marked down units that offered no noise information.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tank and ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tank sizes, drainage and carry handles. The Kismile's 1.1 L tank and the EUHOMY's 1.2 qt tank imply frequent refills. Smooth daily upkeep earned points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value versus compromise
howWeEvaluated.description: Each pick sits in the lower half of the price range. We weighed what each gives up against a premium model, such as quieter running or bigger tanks, and whether that matters for a typical household.

faq.q: Is nugget ice better than cube ice?
faq.a: It is softer, chewable and cools drinks quickly, but it melts faster and dilutes more. Cubes last longer. Choose by how you use ice.

faq.q: Do budget nugget ice makers last?
faq.a: Many last a few years with regular descaling. Scale, noise and pump wear are the typical problems. Filtered water and monthly cleaning extend life.

faq.q: Can I store ice in the machine?
faq.a: Only for short periods. The basket is not a freezer, so ice melts and drains back into the reservoir. For storage, scoop ice into a freezer bag.

faq.q: Why is my machine so loud?
faq.a: The compressor, pump and auger all run during ice-making. Place it on a stable surface and keep it level. Some noise is normal for this type, and a rattle usually means the unit is touching a cabinet or sitting on an uneven spot. Rinsing the basket and checking that the lid is seated can also stop a buzz.

It is strongly recommended. Minerals form scale that clogs the system. Distilled water keeps the machine cleanest but is more expensive. A carbon pitcher filter is a good middle ground, since it improves taste and trims some of the chlorine, though it does not remove hardness.

faq.q: How much ice will I really get?
faq.a: A few pounds an hour at best, with the basket holding only a few pounds. The 24 hour figure assumes the basket is emptied constantly. Plan your use around the basket size. If you host a lot, make ice ahead of time in several rounds and keep it in a freezer bag, then use the machine for top-ups. That workflow gets far more from a small machine than waiting at the counter.
